arXiv:2610.36437v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, a task's primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward: on a failing response, an auxiliary cannot exceed the primary. However, group-relative advantage estimators treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, so it can reverse the primary's order, and at the primary's ceiling only auxiliaries order responses. Keeping gated auxiliaries hurts some tasks, while dropping them hurts others. We propose CONCUR, an advantage estimator that replaces the standardized scores of each gated auxiliary with the closest scores that satisfy two conditions: responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores, and responses at the primary's ceiling receive equal scores. CONCUR-T applies both conditions throughout training, and CONCUR-A lifts the second for an auxiliary that agrees with the primary's order more often than it reverses it among passing responses. On three models from two families and across math, code, instruction following, and writing, both variants score higher on average than all baselines and than when all the gated auxiliaries are dropped.
title: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning

arXiv:2610.36308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

As organizations adopt autonomous agents to build applications, securing identities and access has become more challenging. Developers relying on agents to provision cloud resources, write Terraform, and deploy microservices at machine-speed only find their CI/CD pipelines blocked even faster as security friction scales.  

To help you get ahead of agentic-era Identity and Access Management, today we’re introducing IAM Helper. This suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows. 

As an agent-native orchestration and interface layer for Google Cloud IAM, it augments Google Cloud’s core IAM engines — including Policy Intelligence and Privileged Access Manager (PAM) — making IAM skills callable directly by autonomous code assistants, deployment pipelines, and custom agents. Using this functionality reduces the administrative overhead of maintaining least-privilege security and agent governance, while maximizing utility, and accelerating deployment.

IAM Helper Agent Skills: Fast, secure deployment with automated governance

Manual troubleshooting of permission blockers creates friction for engineering and administrators, while shortcuts can lead to broad agent over-permissioning that puts least privilege at risk. 

IAM Helper empowers agents to handle access management dynamically. It shifts the burden of policy evaluation away from human administrators and LLMs, offloading complex orchestration directly to the Google Cloud backend, to maximize token efficiency and prevent costly operational bottlenecks.

Rather than operating as isolated utilities, IAM Helper Agent Skills guide agents through the cloud access lifecycle. These end-to-end workflows, helper scripts, and guardrails packaged using the open Agent Skills standard can orchestrate multiple underlying functions and APIs to resolve complex IAM tasks. They work across common agents (Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist, ADK, Claude Code, and Cursor). 

Built-in guardrails and real-world impact

Every IAM Helper agent skill separates read-only discovery from policy changes: Diagnostics and simulations run automatically, while any change to access policies pauses for human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation based on customizable risk tiers. To see the value of IAM Helper in practice, consider how it transforms two everyday scenarios:

  • Scaled user-assisted remediation: Suppose a developer's coding agent hits a 403 error while deploying a new application. Rather than filing a support ticket and idling, the agent uses iam-helper-for-troubleshooting to identify the missing Pub/Sub permission in seconds, then uses iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management to request a one-hour JIT grant, eliminating hours of debugging friction.

  • Autonomous pipeline self-healing: An infrastructure agent encounters a permission block during a routine deployment pipeline. Rather than failing the build, the pipeline uses IAM Helper Agent skills to generate a revised, least-privilege policy, verifies against 90 days of logs via iam-helper-for-policy-simulator that active services won't break, and routes the change to an admin for quick approval.

IAM Helper Agent Skills are designed for maximum token and cost efficiency, allowing agents to execute multi-step administrative operations autonomously.

  1. Authoring compliant, least-privilege policies: As DevOps engineers translate access requirements into JSON, YAML, or Terraform HCL, iam-helper-for-policy-management generates and validates IAM v1 allow bindings and IAM v2 deny rules. It automatically catches and blocks risky configs before they are applied, including public access (allUsers) and broad basic roles (roles/owner, roles/editor).

  2. Unblocking 403 errors in seconds: When an on-call engineer or deployment agent hits a cryptic 403 PERMISSION_DENIED error, iam-helper-for-troubleshooting identifies the exact missing permission or blocking rule in seconds. It adapts to the user’s role: Developers can check if they can unblock themselves locally or generate a structured ticket for their administrator (Requester flow), while security administrators can trace inherited allow and v2 deny rules across organization, folder, and project hierarchies to resolve the issue (Resolver flow).

  3. Simulating blast radius before rolling out changes: Before a platform engineer updates a policy or applies IAM Recommender role reductions, they need confidence that active workloads won't break. iam-helper-for-policy-simulator walks the agent through a structured plan, simulate, analyze, and apply flow, testing proposed changes against 90 days of historical access logs to confirm existing traffic won't be disrupted before any update takes effect.

  4. Elevating access just-in-time instead of granting standing privileges: When responders or maintenance agents need temporary production access, iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management manages the lifecycle of on-demand credentials through Privileged Access Manager (PAM). It supports requester, administrator, and approver workflows so elevated access is audited, time-bound, and automatically revoked once the task is done.

While IAM Helper Agent Skills supply the high-level workflow logic, they are all based on a common set of foundational MCP Tools. 

Powered by Google Cloud IAM MCP tools

Google Cloud IAM Helper MCP tools provide the backend connection through atomic, read-only functions exposed via Google-managed MCP servers across core IAM endpoints (Policy Troubleshooter, Policy Analyzer, Policy Simulator, and IAM v1/v2 APIs). 

Rather than requiring teams to write custom API wrappers, MCP tools give agents a standard way to query the cloud backend and get exact answers without parsing verbose policy documents in the prompt, maximizing token efficiency. Agents can dynamically discover and invoke these tools to execute basic operations like checking permissions or listing roles when custom logic is required.

Because operations like hierarchy traversal, group expansion, and policy evaluation happen on dedicated IAM endpoints (spanning IAM v1 allow roles, IAM v2 deny, Policy Troubleshooter, and Policy Analyzer), skills run quickly and accurately with minimal token usage. Teams can also use these atomic MCP tools directly when writing their own custom Agent Skills, making it straightforward to combine Google Cloud's IAM capabilities with internal ticketing systems, custom compliance checks, and existing deployment pipelines.

Getting started

Accelerate your agentic workflows, reduce operational overhead, and bring intelligent, scalable security to your deployment pipelines. Start building with IAM Helper Agent skills today by exploring our Google Cloud Agent Skills Catalog and dive deeper with the official IAM documentation.

Earlier this year, we introduced Gemini Robotics 2 — our next-generation intelligence layer enabling robots to think, act, and adapt in the physical world. At the core of this breakthrough is Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2), a specialized Gemini model that serves as a robot’s high-level brain. Working across any robot embodiment — from stationary arms to full humanoids — Gemini Robotics ER 2 combines advanced spatial and temporal video understanding with long-horizon planning and built-in safety guardrails. This enables robots to converse naturally with humans, orchestrate low-level action models and hardware APIs, execute multi-minute tasks involving hundreds of decisions, and collaborate across multi-robot teams.

Today, we are bringing this same frontier embodied reasoning model to enterprise production environments: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is now available in public preview on the Gemini platform. For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Powering physical agents for enterprise robotics

Gemini Robotics ER 2 transforms a robot into a physical agent. The model combines deep spatio-temporal reasoning and long-horizon planning, enabling robots to orchestrate steps to complete a task, self-correct, and generalize to novel situations. To build an agentic setup, developers can declare low-level control interfaces — like Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models or navigation APIs — as tools, and stream multimodal video, audio, or text directly into the model.

Here is what the model delivers for businesses building and operating robotics:

1. Physical task verification, understanding, and self-correction

In physical operations, a robot needs to know whether a step actually succeeded before moving on to the next one. Gemini Robotics ER 2 adapts to new and unfamiliar situations on the fly by reasoning over continuous video feeds. The model:

  • Classifies task progress into binary status, discrete categories, or continuous scores to improve real-time situational awareness and enable real-time adjustment or iteration on failed steps, without restarting an entire workflow.

  • Pinpoints the exact video frame where a critical event occurs (such as when to stop pouring a liquid) with 91.3% accuracy and a 0.96-second mean absolute frame distance, running at 4x the execution speed and a fraction of the compute cost of many larger model categories.

  • It advances our core spatial reasoning capability, including visual question answering and instrument reading. For example, it can read and interpret values across 10+ instrument categories including circular dials, sight glasses, digital displays, linear scales, rulers, and liquid thermometers directly from visual input.

2. One intelligence layer across any embodiments

Gemini Robotics ER 2 orchestrates robots of many shapes and sizes, scaling its intelligence from stationary arms and wheeled rovers to quadrupeds and complex forms. It also unlocks multi-robot collaboration, allowing different types of robots to share a semantic understanding of their workspace, divide labor, and hand off tasks to complete workflows a single machine could not do alone.

3. Agentic tool orchestration and natural language interaction

Gemini Robotics ER 2 thinks about what comes next while simultaneously orchestrating  actions. Developers can declare low-level control interfaces — such as VLA models, navigation APIs, or custom functions — as tools across simulation, real-world robot control, or human tele-operation. Gemini Robotics ER 2 can orchestrate navigation and manipulator movement APIs from natural language commands, allowing the robot to explain its approach while performing an action, and letting operators redirect it without using technical language.

4. Build safe, adaptive physical agents in Google Cloud

Developers and enterprise teams use the Gemini platform to simulate, orchestrate, and manage physical agents, which are then deployed to run directly on physical robots at the edge using Google Cloud's scalable infrastructure:

  • Simulate fast:  Test robot behaviors before touching hardware by running simulations in familiar environments like MuJoCo-Warp and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Then generate synthetic scenarios with multimodal models and auto-label workcell imagery on the Gemini platform.

  • Train smart: Use Gemini Robotics ER 2's spatial pointing, moment finding, and progress classification to curate and label demonstration videos in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Then train custom Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through the Gemini platform, GKE, or Cluster Director.

  • Operate easily: Deploy Gemini Robotics ER 2 workflows on the Gemini platform with enterprise IAM, security controls, and built-in function calling. Offload latency-sensitive local workloads like SLAM and path planning to factory floors with Google Distributed Cloud, and stream fleet telemetry into BigQuery. arXiv:2610.36013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. Specialist policies alone do not ensure task-level reliability, while powerful multimodal agents rely on costly reasoning and external experience that compact models struggle to reproduce. We introduce OmniBrain-0, a lightweight unified embodied agent that coordinates manipulation and navigation through a shared high-level decision model, integrating task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery. Our progressive training framework combines embodied pretraining, domain-specialized agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). It distills powerful teachers' interaction experience into manipulation and navigation experts, then consolidates their decision capabilities into OmniBrain-0. Unification therefore occurs within the learned decision model rather than only at the tool interface. We further introduce Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), a data flywheel in which a Meta-Agent turns execution evidence into refined rubrics, step-level reminders, and verified trajectories for domain-expert updates before their reconsolidation into OmniBrain-0 through MOPD. We evaluate OmniBrain-0 on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and R2R-CE Val-Unseen, as well as multiple real-world manipulation tasks. OmniBrain-0 combines strong cross-domain task performance with substantially lower inference and execution overhead than its closed-source teacher, demonstrating efficient transfer and consolidation of embodied capabilities into a compact unified agent.
title: OmniBrain-0: A Unified Agentic Model for Embodied Intelligence

arXiv:2610.36191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate fluent yet factually incorrect responses, raising concerns about their reliability. Recent hallucination detectors increasingly exploit internal representations, but extracting informative signals from high-dimensional hidden states remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on selected activations or pooling-based compression, potentially overlooking discriminative information distributed across Transformer layers, feature modes, and tokens. We propose LOTUS (Low-rank Order-statistic TUcker-based Subspace learning), a multilinear low-rank decomposition framework for hallucination detection that extracts compact representations from LLM hidden states while reducing dependence on labeled data. Our approach first summarizes variable-length token representations using complementary statistical descriptors that capture peak activations, activation distributions, and cross-layer changes. We then leverage low-rank multilinear decomposition to extract compact representations that capture the underlying structure of LLM hidden states, which are subsequently used to train a lightweight hallucination classifier. Experiments across multiple LLMs and question-answering benchmarks demonstrate improved hallucination detection performance over recent state-of-the-art baselines.
title: LLM Hallucination Detection via Low-rank Multilinear Decomposition

arXiv:2610.36077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.
title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents

However, repository-specific skills must evolve with changing code structures, implementation conventions, and maintenance requirements. Pull requests (PRs) provide a natural source of such knowledge by recording how repositories evolve through implementation and review. Meanwhile, new PRs must follow repository-specific implementation patterns, modify related components consistently, and ensure that existing tests continue to pass while adding coverage for new functionality. This creates a mutually reinforcing cycle: PRs provide knowledge for updating skills, while these skills improve future PRs, maintain repositories, and support further skill evolution. To enable this co-evolution of PRs, repositories, and skills, we propose Skill Dreaming, a framework that learns from PR streams to guide continuous repository development and maintenance. Given a repository and its PR history, Skill Dreaming builds a repository-specific skill library by extracting executable knowledge from validated PRs and continuously refines the skills as new PR information becomes available. These skills guide coding agents not only in implementing requested features but also in maintaining associated tests, documentation, compatibility, and repository conventions. By integrating PR analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming provides an end-to-end workflow for applying learned skills to repository changes and incorporating subsequent PR outcomes into future skill updates.
title: Skill Dreaming: Evolving Repository Skills through Pull Request Streams

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.36184v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bengali, spoken by over 230 million people, remains severely under-resourced in spoken language research. Existing open Bengali ASR corpora are confined to short, read or crowd-sourced speech and lack speaker diarization and long-form audio.
  We present Lipi-Ghor, a large-scale weakly-supervised Bengali speech corpus comprising 885 hours of audio sourced from 998 YouTube videos across 596 unique channels, spanning 17 diverse domains including audiobooks, drama, religious sermons, news, and regional dialects. Each recording is annotated in SSTT format (Speaker, Speech, Transcription, Timestamp), which combines automated diarization with Bengali YouTube caption tracks.
  To our knowledge, Lipi-Ghor is the first Bengali speech corpus to pair large-scale coverage with speaker-diarized, long-form audio annotations, both of which are absent from existing open Bengali resources. We also present the construction methodology as a replicable pipeline for any language with a sufficient captioned YouTube presence. Targeted channel curation across a handful of rich domains yields corpus scales that were previously out of reach for low-resource languages.
  We benchmark four widely-used ASR models under zero-shot and fine-tuned conditions. All four degrade consistently on emotive, dialectal, and long-form content. Because caption targets are noisy, we also release a human-annotated gold evaluation split, verified by 17 volunteer annotators over 30 hours of human-in-the-loop correction and stratified across all 17 domains.
  We release our original contributions (video-ID lists, diarization output, pipeline code, and the gold annotations) under CC-BY-4.0, and distribute caption-derived transcripts for research use only; no raw audio is redistributed.
title: Lipi-Ghor: A Large-Scale, Diarized, Multi-Domain Bengali Speech Corpus and a Scalable Pipeline for Building It

raw_summary:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now runs the harness and model requests in the same process as your application. Built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

The adapter uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. It no longer needs to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host rather than being forwarded into the sandbox.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.36178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We measure, without sampling error, the probability a language model assigns to each integer from 1 to N when asked for a random number. For a fixed prompt the model defines one probability vector, which we compute by summing over each integer's scored spellings rather than estimate by sampling, removing the noise that limits earlier studies [1, 4]. We evaluate 18 open-weight model lines at five ranges up to N = 100, under 29 decoding configurations, on two inference stacks; 15 of them have matched base and instruction-tuned checkpoints that both give usable answers. Instruction tuning makes the distribution less uniform in all 15 pairs. It installs one heuristic, round-number avoidance, and sharpens another, endpoint avoidance. Base checkpoints do not avoid round numbers once the endpoints are removed from those sets; tuned checkpoints avoid them, multiples of 10 almost completely. Base checkpoints return the endpoints 1 and N at 0.30 to 0.60 of the interior rate; tuned checkpoints almost never return them. A preference for odd numbers is consistent across tuned checkpoints only at N = 100, where base checkpoints also show it weakly. Endpoint avoidance and the odd preference fit the account Kubovy and Psotka [6] proposed for human number choice; round-number avoidance is not part of that account, and the midpoint avoidance it predicts is essentially absent, with one slight exception at N = 100. Tuning does not install a new favourite integer shared across models: above N = 10 no modal integer is shared by more than 42 percent of tuned conditions, and P (17) rises in 10 of 15 pairs and falls in 5. The concentration is present in the model's own distribution: at temperature 1.0, nucleus truncation at top-p 0.95 adds a median of 0.035 to the total variation distance.
title: 3, 7, 14, 17, 42: Instruction Tuning Installs and Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.
title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.36146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prompt optimization should improve the image a user receives without changing the scene the user requested. Yet stylistic rewriting can weaken object attributes and relations even when global text--image similarity remains high. We propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision. The graph exposes what should be preserved, while deletion, reordering, and insertion provide a token-aligned way to modify the prompt. This turns structural feedback from an external critique into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Learning from that signal requires handling both uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. StruPO retains grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple images for each edit before computing group-relative advantages. Experiments span three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, with comparisons to learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control. StruPO improves the faithfulness--aesthetics trade-off, with consistent gains in relational fidelity. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study provide complementary evidence, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity. Controlled ablations connect these gains to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning. The resulting policy produces reusable optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, without an iterative critique--rewrite loop.
title: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.36325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.
title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis

arXiv:2610.36360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present AK_QMUL's submissions to the ArGuard-2026 shared tasks on Arabic harmful-prompt detection: a binary safe/unsafe task (B1) and a seven-way harm-domain task (B2). Both submissions use one backbone -- JAIS-6.7B fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA and a linear classification head over its last-token representation. For B1 we train a four-way head that factors the label by dialect register {safe, unsafe} x {MSA, other}, we augment the training fold with MSA prompts from AraSafe, and decode with a plain argmax to score safe/unsafe. For B2 we fine-tune the same backbone as a seven-way classifier and average the softmax outputs of five random seeds. Both submissions ranked first on their track, with macro-F1 0.984 on B1 and 0.790 on B2. We report results by dialect and by class: on B1 the model is accurate across all six dialects (93.6--99.8%) and its predicted unsafe rate tracks the true rate closely; on B2 six of the seven classes reach F1 between 0.73 and 0.98, with the residual error concentrated in the Bully class, which overlaps semantically with harassment and harm-to-others.
title: AK_QMUL at ArGuard Shared Tasks: A Single Fine-Tuned JAIS for Arabic Harmful-Prompt Detection
